title: Medicine and Physicians
lead: The Bible's doctors and remedies, and the old question of whether going to a doctor shows a lack of faith. Hebrew uses one word, rophe', "healer," both for human doctors and for the LORD himself (Exodus 15:26). This page is about human medicine. Healing by God's direct act is under Healing, and the anointing of the sick under Anointing.

sections.b:
Joseph's servants "the physicians" embalm Jacob in Egypt (Genesis 50:2). The law makes a man who injures another pay for the time lost and see "that he is fully healed" (Exodus 21:19). Balm, Hebrew tsori, was carried from Gilead to Egypt as a trade good and a gift (Genesis 37:25; Genesis 43:11). The prophets use it as a picture of a cure: "Is there no balm in Gilead? Is no healer there?" (Jeremiah 8:22; compare Jeremiah 46:11; Jeremiah 51:8). Which plant gave it is not known for certain. The Greek translators simply wrote rhētinē, "resin."

Other remedies appear in passing. Isaiah has a lump of pressed figs put on King Hezekiah's sore (2 Kings 20:7; Isaiah 38:21). Wounds are "squeezed clean or bandaged / or eased with oil" (Isaiah 1:6). A broken arm should have been bound up (Ezekiel 30:21). The Samaritan "poured oil and wine on his wounds and bandaged them" (Luke 10:34). Paul advises "a little wine for your stomach" (1 Timothy 5:23). Laodicea is told to buy "eye salve" (Revelation 3:18). The Book of Tobit is read as Scripture by Catholic and Orthodox Christians. In it the angel tells Tobias to keep a fish's gall as medicine for eyes (Tobit 6:5–9). Later Tobias puts it on his father's eyes, and his blindness is healed (Tobit 11:11–13).

sections.h: Asa, Job's friends and the doctors of the Gospels
sections.b:
King Asa "fell sick in his feet ... Even in his sickness he did not seek the LORD, only the healers" (2 Chronicles 16:12). The KJV has "physicians." The Hebrew word, rophe'im, is the same one that names God "your healer" in Exodus 15:26. Job calls his friends "healers of nothing" (Job 13:4).

In the Gospels, a woman with a flow of blood had suffered under "many doctors" and "only gotten worse" (Mark 5:26). Paul calls Luke "the beloved doctor" (Colossians 4:14). Luke says that "she had poured her whole livelihood into doctors" and no one could cure her. He does not say she got worse (Luke 8:43). Not every Greek text has Luke's words about doctors; Westcott and Hort's text leaves them out (see the note on Luke 8:43). Jesus takes the doctor as a picture of himself: "People who are strong do not need a doctor. Sick people do" (Matthew 9:12). He also quotes the proverb "Doctor, cure yourself!" (Luke 4:23).

Was Asa's sin going to doctors at all, or going to them instead of God? Jewish teachers answered differently. The Talmud learns from Exodus 21:19 that "permission is granted to a doctor to heal" (Bava Kamma 85a). Ibn Ezra, on that verse, limited the permission to "blows and wounds that are visible on the surface." Illness inside the body, he said, is "in God's hand," and he pointed to Asa. Ramban (on Leviticus 26:11) held that a fully faithful Israel would have no need of a physician. But he held that the Talmud's permission is given to the doctor, who must not refuse a patient who comes to him.

sections.h: Honor the doctor: Sirach and the churches
sections.b:
Sirach 38:1–15 gives the fullest teaching. Sirach is in the Catholic and Orthodox Bibles. In the Greek it tells the reader to honor the physician, because the Lord created him. The Lord created medicines out of the earth, and a sensible person will not despise them. Sirach recalls the wood that made the water sweet (Exodus 15:25). The sick should pray, turn from sin and bring an offering. Then they should give the doctor his place, since doctors too pray to the Lord for success.

How Christians differ. James tells the sick to call the elders: "Let them pray over him, when they have anointed him with oil in the name of the Lord" (James 5:14). The Catholic Church sees in this rite one of the seven sacraments, the Anointing of the Sick (Catechism 1510–1511). The same Catechism (2288) also teaches care for health: "Life and physical health are precious gifts entrusted to us by God. We must take reasonable care of them, taking into account the needs of others and the common good." Pentecostal churches stress that God heals now. Thomas Trask, General Superintendent of the Assemblies of God, wrote that "Divine healing was provided for in the Atonement." How far such healing should be expected today is discussed under Healing.

common: The Bible condemns going to doctors, since Asa "did not seek the LORD, only the healers" (2 Chronicles 16:12).
uncommon: The Talmud finds a doctor's permission to heal in the law about injuries (Exodus 21:19).
Ibn Ezra held that the permission covers only wounds on the surface of the body.
